title: Turing machines
subtitle: An infinite tape, a moving head and a finite rulebook: the simplest machine that can compute anything a computer can.

sections.title: The machine
sections.body: A Turing machine has an infinite tape of cells, a head that reads and writes one cell, and a finite control. Each step: read the symbol, then (depending on state and symbol) write a symbol, move Left, Right or Stay, and change state. It halts in an accepting or rejecting state. Its description is a table of rules state, read → state, write, move.

questions.prompt: What can a Turing machine do that a finite automaton cannot?

choices.text: Write to its tape and revisit cells — unbounded read/write memory.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: That is what makes it a general computer.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.1 — incrementing 1011
figures.note: Binary increment: walk to the right end, then add 1 moving left.

sections.title: Computing with a Turing machine
sections.body: Beyond accepting strings, a TM can compute: the tape at halt is the output. The increment machine turns 1011 (eleven) into 1100 (twelve) and 111 into 1000. In the same style you can build machines for addition, copying, comparison and multiplication; composing them gives any algorithm.

worked.why: Scan right to the blank, step back; 1 + 1 = 0 carry 1, 1 + 1 = 0 carry 1, then 0 + 1 = 1 stop.

questions.prompt: What does the increment machine leave on the tape for input 111?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: All carries propagate to a new leading 1.

sections.title: A decider: palindromes
sections.body: This machine checks whether a string over {a, b} is a palindrome: erase the first symbol, remember it in the state, run to the far end, compare with the last symbol, erase that too, return to the start and repeat. abba → accepted, abb → rejected. A finite automaton cannot do this; neither can a PDA on its own for all palindromes of unknown middle — the TM simply moves back and forth.

questions.prompt: Why does this machine erase symbols as it matches them?

choices.text: Erasing marks what has been checked so the head knows where the unmatched middle begins.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The tape is its working memory.

sections.title: Variants that add no power
sections.body: Multiple tapes, a two-way infinite tape, nondeterminism, a stay move, even extra heads: each can be simulated by a plain single-tape TM (possibly slower). Every reasonable model of computation — lambda calculus, recursive functions, RAM machines — turns out equivalent. That consistency is the evidence behind the Church–Turing thesis.

questions.prompt: Does a two-tape Turing machine recognise more languages than a one-tape one?

choices.text: No — it can be simulated by a single tape, only slower.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Extra tapes change speed, not computability.

sections.title: Unrestricted grammars and the hierarchy
sections.body: Unrestricted (type-0) grammars have productions α → β with no constraint; they generate exactly the recursively enumerable languages, those a TM can accept (possibly running forever on non-members). A TM that always halts decides a recursive language. Type-1 context-sensitive, type-2 context-free and type-3 regular grammars complete the Chomsky hierarchy.

questions.prompt: A language is recursively enumerable if…

choices.text: Some Turing machine accepts exactly its strings (it may loop on others).
A TM decides it and always halts.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A decider must always halt; an acceptor need not.

problems.prompt: Match each class to its machine: regular, context-free, context-sensitive, recursively enumerable.
problems.answer: Regular — finite automaton; context-free — pushdown automaton; context-sensitive — linear-bounded automaton; recursively enumerable — Turing machine.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• TM = finite control + unbounded tape; rules: state, read → state, write, move.
  • It computes functions and decides languages; variants are equivalent.
